### Title: Ask Yourself Nicely

### Content: 
When you want something from a stranger, you know you must be kind in making the ask. Of yourself, however, you demand instant performance. You lie awake at night, berating yourself: “Go back to sleep, you idiot!” Why not try what has worked flawlessly with other people for decades?
“Dear me, I know you’re tired, but I’d love it if you could just get a few more hours of rest. I’ll be here to cheer you on in the morning!”
“Dear me, I know you’re scared, but I’d love it if you could just hit ‘publish.’ You’ve done it before, and you’ll do it again!”
“Dear me, I know you’re sad, but I’d love it if you could just get out of bed. The sun is waiting to greet you.”
When you’re your own best friend, you’ll treat yourself like one. And even if you don’t always succeed, at least you’ll always be nice.

### Title: Silent Acknowledgement

### Content: 
I can’t reply to every comment I get online. I can’t congratulate every friend on every LinkedIn update. These days, I sometimes can’t even answer every WhatsApp message.
But I see them. I see all of them. And I acknowledge them. Silently. I don’t know whether this is enough, but it is something. Something I can do. I’m not ignoring you. I’m not indifferent to your success. I’m just busy. As busy as you are. As busy as we all are.
I’m not sure how much silent acknowledgement you’re receiving, but I hope you get some. I hope you’ll remember to send it to others. And I hope you’ll always find the time to give your loved ones the real thing.

### Title: The Backstory Is the Story

### Content: 
Tolkien’s Silmarillion is a masterpiece. Not because of how well it is written, how coherent the story, or how illustrious its characters. It is a work of genius because Tolkien actually took the time, thought, and care to craft 5,000 years of backstory to his main works, The Hobbit and The Lord of the Rings.
5,000 years! That’s 1,000 years for every 100 pages of The Lord of the Rings. That’s 10 times the entire history of Western civilization. What Tolkien did was not just create a story. He created a world.
The Silmarillion is a book of legends, and it is exactly what makes the world of The Lord of the Rings feel so real. It’s the backdrop against which the main story unfolds. It’s the history, the culture, the beliefs, the values, the stories of the people. It’s the very air the characters breathe, and that’s why they feel so alive. It’s why we can feel them breathe too.
The Silmarillion is not just the backstory to The Lord of the Rings. It is the story. Without it, there’d be no story at all. Just a bunch of words on a page, no meaning, no context, no life.
The Silmarillion is the story because the backstory is always the story. What happened before is what makes what’s happening now interesting.
Your life is a story. It’s a story in the making, and every day, you get to decide what you’ll write. You get to decide what happens next. But what happens next is only as good as what happened before.
The backstory is the story. Never forget it.

### Title: It’s Okay If the Glass Breaks

### Content: 
Donna Berzatto has been anything but a reliable mother to her three children. But when her only daughter Natalie, nicknamed “Sugar,” is about to give birth, the soon-to-be grandmother becomes an unexpected pillar of support.
With the baby’s father nowhere to be found, Sugar must make a tough decision: Will she give her child up for adoption? Or will she raise it on her own?
Donna is there to help her through it all. She even offers to move in with her daughter for a while. But when Sugar is finally ready to leave the hospital, she asks her mom to bring her a glass of water. Donna leaves the room, and on her way to the water fountain, she breaks the glass. She panics and runs away.
It’s a moment that perfectly encapsulates Donna’s life: She’s just about to get it right when everything falls apart. And while it’s a moment that’s easy to laugh off, it’s also one that’s easy to miss.
If you’ve ever dropped a glass of water, you know the feeling. It’s a small mistake, but it feels like a big one. It’s an accident that feels like a crime. “How could I be so stupid?” we ask ourselves. “How could I let this happen?”
But the truth is, it’s okay if the glass breaks. It’s okay if we make mistakes. It’s okay if we’re not perfect. It’s okay if we’re not always there for our children. It’s okay if we don’t always have the right words. It’s okay if we don’t always know what to do.
What matters is that we try. What matters is that we show up. What matters is that we’re there for our children when they need us. What matters is that we’re willing to learn from our mistakes. What matters is that we’re willing to change.
It’s okay if the glass breaks. It’s okay if we’re not perfect. What matters is that we keep trying. That we keep showing up. That we keep learning. That we keep changing.

### Title: Billion-Dollar Bullshit

### Content: 
From 2014 to 2017, Juicero collected a whopping $120 million in funding from venture capitalists. The company then applied “the Silicon Valley formula” to its product, a juice dispenser. They made a sleek-looking machine that pressed juice made of fresh, local ingredients from specifically designed and verified packets. They charged $400 for that machine. They launched exclusively in California and only sold to customers via a subscription model. And a few months later, they shut down and failed.
It’s easy to laugh at Juicero’s failure, but it’s also easy to see why investors were convinced: The team was strong. The product was high-tech. The branding was on point. And the business model was sound. It’s a classic case of “seemed like a good idea at the time,” and that’s what makes it so fascinating.
I don’t think Juicero was a scam. I think they were just trying to do what every startup tries to do: Make something that works and that people want. But sometimes, you don’t know what you’re doing. Sometimes, you can’t see what’s right in front of you. And sometimes, you’re just plain wrong.
The company’s founder, Doug Evans, had a vision: He wanted to make fresh juice available to everyone. He wanted to put a juicer in every home. He wanted to create a new standard for how we consume food. But in trying to do all that, he missed the forest for the trees. Juicero’s packets cost $5 to $8. That’s $5 to $8 for a single glass of juice. It’s more expensive than the juice you can buy in the store, and it’s more expensive than the juice you can make yourself.
Evans was so focused on his vision that he forgot to ask himself the most important question: Why would anyone buy this? And that’s why Juicero failed.
It’s easy to get caught up in the hype. It’s easy to get swept away by the momentum. But it’s important to remember that, at the end of the day, you’re still selling a product. And if that product doesn’t solve a problem for your customer, it’s not going to sell. No matter how much money you raise, no matter how much hype you generate, and no matter how much you believe in your vision.
In business, there’s a saying: “You can’t polish a turd.” It means that no matter how much you try to dress up a bad product, it’s still going to be a bad product. And that’s what Juicero was. A turd. A $120 million turd.
It’s a cautionary tale for all of us. A reminder that, no matter how much money we raise, no matter how much hype we generate, and no matter how much we believe in our vision, we still need to ask ourselves the most important question: Why would anyone buy this? And if we can’t answer that question, we’re just peddling billion-dollar bullshit.

### Title: Pretend It’s the Last Time

### Content: 
My sister once reminded me that there are plenty of last times we miss. The last time we hang out with a friend before our paths twist in separate directions. The last time we have a certain food before we leave a place we’ll never revisit. Sometimes, we might even fail to recognize the last phone call with someone we love before they die. That’s why “this might be the last time” is a thought worth having on occasion.
It’t a thought to have all the time. If you did, you’d be paralyzed. It’s not the kind of idea you can hold on to. You can only drop it in your brain and see where it lands. Let it rest for a while. Then, it will make its way. You’ll be reminded to call your friend. You’ll eat a certain dish at a certain restaurant. You’ll take a picture of your grandfather while he’s asleep.
The idea is to remember without remembering. To allow the thought to do its work without forcing it. That’s what I’m doing right now. I’m not trying to make you do anything. I’m just writing. You’re just reading. And yet, if you think about it, this might be the last time you read one of my posts.
You can’t know, of course. But it’s a possibility. And if it’s the last time, I want you to know that I’m grateful. Grateful you came here. Grateful you read my writing. Grateful you spent some of your time with me. And if you never come back, I’ll be sad, but I’ll also be happy. Happy that I got to write this post. Happy that I got to say thank you. Happy that I got to pretend it was the last time.

### Title: A Body Is Just a Shell

### Content: 
When his son Dino died at just 24 years old, the great Enzo Ferrari learned that engineers can’t fix bodies. In the world of Alita: Battle Angel, the opposite is true: With most people being at least partially cyborg, Dr. Dyson Ido, played by Christoph Waltz, repairs bodies all day long.
When he finds the head and torso of a cyborg girl in a scrapyard, he gives her a new body, and Alita is born. Alita has no memories, and she must learn everything from scratch. In a way, she is like a child, and so Dr. Ido becomes her father.
As Alita grows into her new life, she discovers her body is more than just a shell. It is a powerful weapon, and she can use it to fight for what’s right. But she must also learn to protect her heart.
In a scene that mirrors the moment when Dino Ferrari was diagnosed with Duchenne muscular dystrophy, Alita is told by her doctor that she has a “weak heart.” She can’t have a new one. She’ll have to make do with what she has. Just like Dino, Alita is told she can’t have the one thing she needs most. And just like Enzo, Dr. Ido is helpless in the face of his daughter’s pain.
But Alita is not Dino. She is a cyborg. And cyborgs can fix bodies. Alita may not be able to get a new heart, but she can get a new body. And she does.
In the end, Alita learns that a body is just a shell. It’s what’s inside that counts. And she uses her new body to fight for what she believes in.
Alita: Battle Angel is a story about identity, love, and loss. It’s a story about what it means to be human. And it’s a story about hope.
Hope that even when our bodies fail us, we can still find a way to fight for what’s right. Hope that even when we lose the people we love, we can still find a way to keep going. And hope that even when the world seems to be falling apart, we can still find a way to hold on to what’s important.
Alita: Battle Angel is a movie about finding hope in the darkest of times. And that’s why it’s a movie worth watching.

### Title: It’s Your Response-Ability

### Title: Creativity as a Well

### Content: 
Sometimes, I happen to draft article ideas during my meditation, and sometimes, all 15 minutes of endurance training go to that activity. That’s not ideal, but it, too, teaches me a lesson: If I spend as little as a quarter of an hour brainstorming, thinking through the past 24 hours, about what happened this week, and allowing my mind to resurface whichever thought it prefers, I have article ideas out the wazoo.
After 15 minutes of reflection, I can write down a dozen ideas, and I can do that every day. I can’t write 12 articles every day, of course, but I can write one. And if I don’t, I can do it again tomorrow. I can do it again every day. I can do it again until the end of time, and that’s the magic of creativity: It’s not a well you can run dry.
The more you draw from it, the more it wants to give you. It’s a well of infinite water, and the only thing that can stop the flow is you. You can stop pulling water from the well. You can forget to take a drink. You can turn away from it and walk in a different direction. But as long as you’re there, standing next to the well, it will always provide for you.
It’s easy to forget this. It’s easy to think that, on any given day, you don’t have anything to say. But you do. You always have something to say. You always have something to write. You always have something to offer. The question is: Are you willing to pull it out? Are you willing to draw it from the well?
It’s not always easy, but it’s always worth it. It’s always worth the effort. And even if you only have 15 minutes to spend, you can still draw something from the well. You can still come up with a dozen ideas, or a single one. You can still write a sentence, or a paragraph, or an entire article. It’s always worth the effort.
So don’t forget the well. Don’t forget to drink from it. And don’t forget that it’s always there for you.

### Title: Dust Walls

### Content: 
A few weeks ago, I was scheduling dozens of posts from the blog to republish them elsewhere. Copy, paste, pick date, hit the button, repeat.
The process was simple, but it took a while. When I was done, I looked at the big calendar and saw the blue dots for each post. They looked like little dust particles on a wall, and I thought: “I just wiped the dust off this wall.”
Sometimes, you’ll have to clean the same wall twice. That’s okay. It’s part of the job. But it’s also nice to look at the wall once you’re done. To see the dust particles neatly lined up in front of you. “Look! I did this. I wiped the dust off this wall.”
The next time you have a repetitive task to do, remember: You’re not just cleaning a wall. You’re cleaning a wall made of dust. That’s worth something.

### Title: Mapping the Terrain

### Content: 
“Where does that door lead again?” Confusion arose in yesterday’s gaming session. My girlfriend held the controller for The Legend of Zelda: Echoes of Wisdom. As part of her turn, she had stormed headlong into a new dungeon. I kept asking her to backtrack, but that was not her style. “No, no, no, just keep going!”
Once we were deep inside the maze, however, we had to backtrack. “Wait, was this the left or the right door? Which one did we come from?” After a few wrong turns, I finally pulled up the map. “Oh, yeah, we’re here.” With the terrain properly mapped, we could move forward once more.
The map is always there. We just have to remember to pull it up. It’s a good thing to do before you start a new quest, but it’s never too late to do it mid-adventure. Just remember to check the map, and you’ll always have a rough idea of where you’re going.
The map is not the territory, but it’s still a useful tool. Use it.

### Title: Driving a T-Rex

### Content: 
I used to visit a friend’s house after school in the 90s. We played Need for Speed 2 on his computer. Thanks to a bunch of cheat codes, you could turn the game from a challenging car race into a completely ridiculous experience. I distinctly remember driving a T-rex around a Hollywood studios–inspired track at 200+ kilometers per hour. It was insane—but also insanely fun.
After a few hours of T-rex-driving, however, I would get bored. “What else can I do here?” I’d think. “How can I get more from this game?” But of course, there was nothing more to get. It was a game that was over. I had won it. I had done everything there was to do. I just didn’t know it yet. So I kept playing. And playing. And playing. Until I was sick of it.
Sometimes, I think we do the same thing in life. We find the cheat codes. We hit the jackpot. We become the master of our domain. And then we keep playing the same game. Why? Because we’re used to it. Because we’re comfortable. Because it’s safe. But sooner or later, we’ll get bored. We’ll feel like we’re stuck in a loop. And then we’ll wonder why we’re not happy.
The truth is, there’s always another game to play. Another challenge to take on. Another adventure to go on. But we have to be willing to let go of the old game. To give up the comfort and safety of what we know. And that’s not easy. But it’s necessary if we want to keep growing.
So when you find yourself driving a T-rex, remember: There’s always another game to play. Don’t be afraid to let go of the old one.

### Title: Big Waves Take Time

### Content: 
Let’s say you’re starting a job after ten years of self-employment. That’s a big shift. As you look back on a decade of work, you realize what felt like a trip through the jungle was actually baking a layer cake, with many artifacts now remaining. But what will you do with them? All those websites and email signup forms and social profiles.
You could delete them all. You could shut down the whole thing. But that feels wrong. You’ve worked so hard to build these things. You can’t just let them go. So you keep them. You consolidate. You set up a new website, and you move everything over. You’re still not done, but at least now, you have a new home base.
The next day, you wake up and realize: “Oh, I can’t just shut it all down.” So you go back to work. You keep consolidating. You keep cleaning up the mess. It’s not the mess you thought you’d be cleaning up, but it’s a mess nonetheless. And you can’t just let it sit there.
The next day, you realize: “Oh, I can’t just leave my email list alone.” So you start emailing them again. You tell them what you’re up to. You let them know about the new website. You send them a few more things. Maybe you’ll even start a new project. Or a new business. Who knows?
But the point is, you can’t just walk away from ten years of work. Not without feeling like you’ve left something behind. So you keep going. You keep working. You keep baking that layer cake.
And that’s the thing about big waves: They take time. You can’t just catch them and ride them. You have to wait for them. You have to paddle out and sit there. And sometimes, you’ll have to wait a long time. But eventually, the wave will come. And when it does, you’ll be ready.
So don’t give up. Don’t walk away. Keep baking that layer cake. Keep paddling out. And eventually, the big wave will come.

### Title: Flick It Again

### Content: 
We have a big cuddle blanket on our couch. It’s massive. Two by two meters or so. In the winter, we use it every night, and every morning, I fold it back into shape.
To’t fold a blanket properly. You have to flick it. The right amount of momentum will allow you to fold it in half, and then in half again, and then in half again. Until you have a neat little package that fits back into its place.
I’ve been folding blankets for over 30 years, and yet, I still have to flick it again. The first flick is never enough. It’s always the second one that gets the blanket to fold neatly. It’s a good reminder: Don’t be afraid to flick it again. To try once more. To give it another go. You might have to do it two, three, four times, but eventually, you’ll get there.
Whether it’s a blanket, a project, or a relationship, don’t be afraid to flick it again.

### Title: An Eternity for a Steppenwolf

### Content: 
A “Steppenwolf” is a kind of wolfhound, half wild animal, half domesticated pet. In Hermann Hesse’s novel of the same name, protagonist Harry claims to be a specimen of this very variety, forever torn between a life outside society’s expectations and the comfort of hiding his lofty ideals in plain sight: among pubs, discussions about politics, and everything else mundane.
During one of his many drunken escapades, Harry meets a mysterious woman named Hermine, who, after much prodding, eventually agrees to help him find the “magic theater” he’s looking for. It is a place where he can see all his dreams and nightmares, and thus, hopefully, finally attain some peace.
One night, Hermine tells Harry she has found the theater, and they set off together. When they arrive at the venue, Harry is surprised to find a small, shabby, run-down shack. He is about to give up on the whole thing when Hermine reminds him: “Magic Theater — Not for everyone.” It is only then that he realizes: The magic is not in the theater. It is in him. He has the power to make this experience magical, regardless of the setting.
Once he enters the building, Harry finds himself in a series of rooms, each of which holds a new, fantastical experience. There is a room where he can relive his childhood, a room where he can see his ex-lover, and a room where he can even see himself, the Steppenwolf, as a wolf, hunting for prey. As he moves through the rooms, Harry realizes that the theater is not just a place for him to see his dreams and nightmares. It is a place for him to confront them, to face his fears and to make peace with his past.
Eventually, Harry finds himself in a room where he can see his own death. He is terrified, but Hermine is there to comfort him. She tells him that death is not the end, but a new beginning. She tells him that he will be reborn, and that he will have a chance to start over. Harry is skeptical, but Hermine insists that he trust her. She tells him that he must let go of his fear and embrace the unknown.
As Harry stands in the room, he can feel the weight of his past lifting off his shoulders. He can feel the burden of his regrets and his mistakes being washed away. He is ready to let go of his old self and to become someone new.
Just then, a door opens in the room, and Harry sees a bright light. He knows that this is the light of rebirth, and he steps through the door. As he does, he feels a surge of energy and a sense of freedom. He is no longer the Steppenwolf, torn between two worlds. He is a new person, ready to face the future with courage and hope.
Harry’s journey through the magic theater is a metaphor for the journey of self-discovery that we all must take. It is a reminder that the magic is not in the world around us, but in ourselves. We have the power to make our own lives magical, regardless of the circumstances.
The magic theater is not a place for everyone. It is a place for those who are willing to confront their fears and to make peace with their past. It is a place for those who are ready to let go of their old selves and to become someone new.
If you are feeling lost or stuck, remember that the magic is within you. You have the power to create your own magic, and to make your life a beautiful and meaningful journey. All you have to do is step through the door and embrace the unknown.
The next day, Harry wakes up in Hermine’s bed. She is gone, but he can feel her presence all around him. He knows that he will never forget her, and that she will always be a part of him. He gets up and looks out the window. The sun is shining, and the world looks full of possibility. He is ready to face the day, and to continue his journey through life.
Harry’s story is a reminder that life is not just a series of events. It is a journey of self-discovery, and it is up to us to make it magical. We have the power to create our own destiny, and to shape our own lives. All we have to do is believe in ourselves, and to trust in the magic that is within us.
If you are feeling lost or stuck, remember that the magic is within you. You have the power to create your own magic, and to make your life a beautiful and meaningful journey. All you have to do is step through the door and embrace the unknown.

### Title: Helping Is a Decision

### Content: 
This morning, my girlfriend and I needed a quick snack before a big event. There were no bakeries near our hotel, and we didn’t have time for a full breakfast. When she went down and asked if we could purchase two croissants or so, the lady said: “Oh, just grab a plate and take whatever! No charge.”
It was a small gesture, but it made our day. It’s not every day someone makes your day, but every day, someone has a chance to make someone’s day. The question is: Will you take it?
Helping is a decision. You can choose to do it. Choose to do it often. Choose to do it even when it’s not in your job description. Choose to do it even when you don’t expect anything in return. Choose to do it when it’s inconvenient. Choose to do it when it’s hard. Choose to do it when it’ll take a long time. Choose to do it when it’s scary. Choose to do it when it’s not the easy way out. Choose to do it when it’s not the popular thing to do. Choose to do it when no one will know you did it. Choose to do it when you think it won’t work. Choose to do it when you think it won’t matter. Choose to do it when you know it will matter.
Helping is a decision. Choose to make it.

### Title: Life Is Not a Simulation

### Content: 
The movie Sully deals with the complications of becoming a hero. To the public, the situation was obvious: Chesley Sullenberger landed a jet plane with no functioning engines on the Hudson river and saved 155 people’s lives—give the man a medal, and let’s be grateful for some good news.
According however, it wasn’t so simple. The NTSB, the National Transportation Safety Board, was tasked with investigating the incident. They ran simulations of the event, and the simulations suggested Sully could have made it back to the airport. In other words, he didn’t need to land on the Hudson at all. He could have saved the plane. “If you could do it, why didn’t you?”
Sully, however, was not so sure. “No matter what any of these simulations say, I know the truth. I was there. It happened to me. I saw the plane. I saw the co-pilot fight for control. I saw the fuel gauge. I saw the airspeed indicator. I saw the bird strike. I saw it all.”
The NTSB, however, was not so sure. “The truth is, you did not have to ditch in the water. You could have landed at LaGuardia.”
“Can you guarantee that those are the only two outcomes?” Sully asked.
“No, but it’s the only two that we can model.”
“Then I cannot talk to you about any of this.”
When the NTSB ran the simulations again, this time with a 35-second delay to mimic the time it took Sully and his co-pilot to make their decision, the planes crashed every time. Sully was right. There was no other option.
The NTSB was so obsessed with the simulation, they forgot the simulation was not reality. They did not see the plane. They did not see the co-pilot fight for control. They did not see the fuel gauge. They did not see the airspeed indicator. They did not see the bird strike. They did not see it all.
The NTSB was not there. Sully was. The truth is that life is not a simulation. It is not a movie. It is not a game. It is not a puzzle, and it is not a test. Life is life, and it only happens once.
You don’t get to do it again. You don’t get to run a simulation. You don’t get to see the bird strike, the fuel gauge, the airspeed indicator, and then decide: “I think I’ll do it again, but this time, I’ll land at LaGuardia.” You have one chance, and you must take it. You must make your decision, and then you must live with the consequences.
Don’t forget that life is not a simulation. Don’t let anyone tell you that you could have done it better. You did your best, and that’s all we can ask of you.

### Title: Appreciate the Basics

### Content: 
Today, our apartment has no water for eight hours. The irony? Outside, it’s raining all day long. But there’s a difference between water coming out of the sky or the ground and fresh H2O pouring out of your tap, and you only realize how big of a difference it is when you’re left without your usual conveniences.
Couldand you fill it with water from the rain, it’ll be a different kind of water than the kind you usually drink. It’s less filtered, less processed, and it’s also less safe to drink. It’s also a lot of work to collect, and you’ll have to boil it to make it safe. That’s a lot of steps for something that, usually, just flows effortlessly from your tap.
It’s easy to forget how much we depend on the basics when we have them. We don’t think about the water we drink, the food we eat, and the electricity we use. We don’t think about the roads we drive on, the phones we talk on, and the internet we browse. But when any one of these things is taken away, we realize how much we depend on them.
The next time you turn on the tap and water comes out, take a moment to appreciate it. The next time you flick a switch and the lights come on, take a moment to appreciate it. The next time you open your fridge and see food, take a moment to appreciate it.
Appreciate the basics. They’re not so basic after all.

### Title: The Demand Was Just Too Big

### Content: 
The customer in front of me kept asking the barista about their café’s expansion. One tiny corner shop had turned into a three-room venue already, replete with a bakery and a space to give classes. Now, they had opened another, even bigger location elsewhere in town. How did they do it? All the barista could do was shrug: “Beats me. It’s such a saturated market. But the demand was just too big.”
Usually, when you start a business, you’re told to go into an unsaturated market. That’s where the money is. That’s where you can grow fast and dominate a new terrain. But what if you’re in a saturated market and, despite the odds, you still win? What if the demand is just too big? That’s a different kind of success, but it’s still success.
The coffee shop in question has a unique blend, a unique look, and a unique way of serving their drinks. Their coffee is delicious. That’s why, in a town of 200,000 people, where every block has at least one café, they can still expand and thrive. The demand was just too big.
In a world where every niche is filled, it’s hard to find a blue ocean. Most of us are swimming in red ones. But that doesn’t mean you can’t make a splash. It just means you have to be unique. You have to be different. You have to be better. And when you are, the demand will be just too big.
It’s okay to be in a crowded market. Just make sure you’re the one everyone wants to buy from.

### Title: The Kite and the Line

### Content: 
The Crain family is anything but a normal family, mostly because they lived in an anything-but-normal house. At one point in the spooky TV series telling their tale, however, the estranged father Hugh shares some advice with his son that works just as well for normal people as it does for those haunted by the ghosts of the past: If you’re a kite, find your line—and vice versa.
“Your mother and I, we were always meant to be together. We were like a kite and a string. And if you cut the string, the kite goes free. But it also falls to the ground. It can’t stay up in the air without the string.”
Hugh and his wife Olivia had a unique connection. They understood each other on a level few couples ever will. But then, they also had a unique dis connection. They could barely stand each other. They fought, they bickered, and they never seemed to agree. The result? A family torn apart, a house left abandoned, and a lot of trauma for everyone involved.
If you’re a kite, find your line. If you’re a line, find your kite. Without each other, you’re both just lying on the ground, and even though you can’t fly without the other, you’ll also never be able to fly as high as you could on your own. It’s a tradeoff, and sometimes, it’s a tradeoff worth making.
I have a kite friend. We’re not as connected as Hugh and Olivia, but we’re still a kite and a line. We can’t always go to the same places at the same time, but we can always rely on one another. We have a unique connection, but we also have a unique dis connection. We can’t stay up in the air without the other, but we also can’t stay up in the air together. That’s the nature of the relationship, and it’s a relationship worth keeping.
Sometimes, your kite will be your partner. Sometimes, it’ll be your best friend. And sometimes, it’ll be a coworker or even your boss. Who you’re connected to is not as important as how you’re connected to them. Are you a kite and a line? Or just two kites, floating in the air? Whatever you are, be it. Live your connection. And when the connection is gone, let it go.
It’s okay to be a kite without a line. It’s okay to be a line without a kite. But when you are one or the other, remember: You can’t fly without the other, but you can’t fly as high as you could on your own. It’s a tradeoff, and sometimes, it’s a tradeoff worth making.

### Title: Experiences Don’t End

### Content: 
Yesterday, I met someone at a party who, as it turned out, was in my year during undergrad. Same college. Same classes. Same exams. “Oh, but you must have never studied at the library then,” she said. “Actually, I was in the library all the time, often from 7 AM to 10 PM,” I responded. “Ahh, that’s why—I always went at night!”
“How funny,” I thought. “We were both there, but we never saw each other.” The next morning, I learned that she was also at the library all day on most days. She just never saw me. “What a coincidence!” I thought. “We were both there, but we never saw each other.”
It’s a nice reminder that experiences don’t end. We don’t always see everything, and that’s okay. It’s never too late to learn, and there’s always more to find out.
Don’t rush to the end of the story. You can always come back to it later—and when you do, you might find it has changed.

### Title: Anxiety Blankets

### Content: 
Asked why he went back to drinking coffee after living without it for 30 days and seeing many benefits, Tim Ferriss said : “I use coffee as a security blanket when my life gets hit with something unpredictable or things seem a little out of control. So even though I realize, intellectually, that it’s counterproductive […], my response to feeling a little anxious is to want coffee—even though it increases anxiety physiologically.”
I, too, have anxiety blankets. I eat too much. I buy too many books. I drink too much coffee. I overwork. I also have positive anxiety blankets, like reading, meditating, and exercising. But sometimes, the negative ones win.
Anxiety blankets are like any habit: You can’t avoid them entirely, but you can try to replace them with better ones. The question is whether we can spot them before they take hold. Can we catch ourselves on the way to the fridge? Can we remember to meditate before we grab our phone? And if we can’t, can we at least have the courage to stop in the middle of it?
The best way to not fall off a cliff is to not get too close to the edge—but if you do, remember that you can always turn around.

### Title: Ride the Schoolbus

### Content: 
The first train connection from my parents’ house to a larger city where I transfer runs through the middle of nowhere. The second stop is a town with a school. Often, many kids get on the tiny, two-wagon train. So for the next 40 minutes, I’ll sit there, tucked away quietly between three dozen high schoolers, listening to their laughter and conversations. I always learn something.
Yesterday,’t a big one, but it’s still worth sharing: “I’m so tired. I just want to go home and watch a movie.” I’m sure every one of us has said this at some point. But what struck me was the “just.” It’s a word we use to diminish the importance of what we’re about to say. “I’m just a teacher.” “It’s just a cold.” “I just want to watch a movie.” But actually, those are all big things.
I’m a teacher. I have a cold. I want to watch a movie. Those are all fine. You don’t have to “just” them. You can just say them as they are. It’s okay. You don’t need to downplay your desires. You don’t have to apologize for your dreams. You can simply state them, and then go about making them happen.
So when I get off the train, I thank the kids for their lesson. I’m sure they don’t know they taught me anything, but that’s how life is. You never know who you’ll touch when. So always be your best self, and remember: Don’t “just” anything. You’re not just a teacher. You’re not just a writer. You’re not just a cashier. You’re a teacher. You’re a writer. You’re a cashier. And you’re awesome.

### Title: Early Following Is Leading

### Content: 
In 2010, Derek Sivers gave a short-and-sweet TED talk that changed my understanding of leadership forever. Showing a short clip of a shirtless guy dancing by himself at a music festival, Derek explains: “First, a leader needs the guts to stand out and be ridiculed.” Well, that part I knew. It’s the part every movie, book, interview, and case study explains over and over again.
In the video, however, a second guy soon joins the dancing dude. “The first follower is what transforms a lone nut into a leader,” Derek says. “If the leader is the flint, the first follower is the spark that makes the fire.” As soon as the second guy shows up, a third, fourth, and fifth follow. Then, all hell breaks loose. A massive crowd of people joins the lone nut, and the dance party is in full swing.
The second follower, Derek explains, is the one who turns the first follower into a follower. It signals that it’s now safe to hop on the bandwagon, and so more and more people do. “Now, here come two more people, and immediately, more. Three is a crowd, and a crowd is news.” As the crowd grows, more and more people will jump on, and the movement will become bigger and bigger.
“If you really care about starting a movement, have the courage to follow and show others how to follow,” Derek says. “When you find a lone nut doing something great, have the guts to be the first person to stand up and join in.” The most important part of leadership, Derek claims, is creating more leaders.
In a world where every individual has the power to start a movement, leadership is no longer just reserved for a few people at the top. Anyone can lead. Anyone can follow. Anyone can be a lone nut, a first follower, or a second follower. What matters is that we keep the chain going. We keep the fire going. We keep the movement going.
Early following is leading. It takes guts to be the first person to clap in the room, but if you believe in something, that’s what you must do. You must show others how to follow, and then you must show others how to lead.
Don’t wait for someone else to take the first step. Don’t wait for someone else to start a movement. If you can’t find a lone nut, be a lone nut. If you can’t find a first follower, be a first follower. And if you can’t find a second follower, be a second follower. You never know when a spark will catch fire, but if you don’t provide any sparks, there won’t be any fire at all.
If you care about starting a movement, have the courage to follow. Have the courage to lead.

### Title: Connecting Is Leading

### Content: 
My friend Mike hates giving presentations. He doesn’t enjoy being the center of attention in a group of people. He’d also be the last to volunteer to do role plays at work. Despite this, nobody I know would hesitate to call Mike a leader. In his own words, he just “ leads from behind.”
Mike is a connector. He knows everyone, and everyone knows him. He’s always happy to make an introduction. “You should meet this person. You guys would get along great.” He’s not afraid to point out when someone is doing a good job, and he’ll always try to help you when you’re stuck. He’ll even do it behind the scenes if he knows you don’t like the spotlight.
Mike is a leader because he connects people. That’s all it takes. You don’t have to be the star of the show to be a leader. You don’t have to give presentations, and you don’t have to be the face of the company. You can be a connector, and you can do it from behind.
There are many ways to be a leader. Connecting is one of them. Don’t let anyone tell you otherwise.

### Title: The 3 Kinds of Eternity

### Content: 
Harry, the antihero of Hermann Hesse’s Steppenwolf, suffers a prolonged, fundamental identity crisis. One idea that gives him comfort is the concept of eternity, which various supporting characters define anew for him in illustrious ways.
There, of course, all turn out to be true. The first one is what we might call “the eternity of the moment.”
“I am in God and God is in me. Only Thou art real, Thou my God, Lord of my life; and when I cease to exist then Thou wilt exist, then Thou art. I am in Thee and Thou art in me. When I no longer exist, my love will be in the air. And after love there can no longer be any names.”
This is the eternity of the mystic, the monk, the person who has renounced the world in order to find a higher plane of existence. It is the kind of eternity that is achieved in the moment, by letting go of the self and becoming one with the universe.
The second is “the eternity of the self.”
“Man is not by any means of fixed and enduring form (this, by the way, is something that people who set a high value on form and formalities, and think they know of such things, do not know and do not even suspect). Man is an entanglement of roots, fibres and currents, which admit of no representation in linear form. Man is a knot, a tangled web, a gyrating torch. Man is a crossroads where natural energies and meanings fight and progressive and reactionary forces clash. What rises on this stage is reality, the stunning precision of the picture, which the great masters knew how to glorify. But every scene lacks the dimension of depth, and no one who walks this stage draws nearer to us or to himself.”
This is the eternity of the artist, the creator, the person who tries to capture the world in all its complexity and beauty. It is the kind of eternity that is achieved by leaving a mark on the world, by creating something that will outlast the self.
The third is “the eternity of the spirit.”
“Every man’s life represents a road toward himself, an attempt at such a road, the intimation of a path. No man has ever been entirely and completely himself. Yet each one strives to become that — one in an obscure way, another in a more clear-sighted manner. Each man represents a failed attempt or a partial success. The man who comes nearest to this goal is the man who can be described as the individual, the one seeking the way in himself. But even the individual, the man we call artist, poet or religious man, is no more than an attempt, a mission; and even if he is the man most nearly approaching completion he still requires an immense amount of interpretation, since he is, and always will be, obscure to himself. But he is a way, an experiment, a transition, and he is not subject to the laws of reason and of calculation.”
This is the eternity of the philosopher, the scientist, the person who tries to understand the world and the self. It is the kind of eternity that is achieved by leaving a legacy of thought, by contributing to the collective understanding of the world.
Which kind of eternity will you choose?

### Title: One Does Not Love Breathing

### Content: 
Scout is smart for her age. By the time she goes to school, she can already read. Her teacher, instead of being amazed, sees her as a threat—to the other children but also to herself. When she is told to “tell her father to stop teaching her at home,” which he never has, she realizes for the first time: “What I have is precious, and there are people out there who’d take it away from me.”
It’s a moment that breaks her heart, but it’s also the moment when she realizes she has something worth protecting. “One does not love breathing,” Scout says in To Kill a Mockingbird. “It’s a habit.”
The first time you’re told your habit is not worth having, you’ll realize how much it means to you. It’s not until someone tries to take it away that you’ll know you must protect it.

### Title: Two Hamsters in the Background

### Content: 
We had some friends over for coffee and cake. Instead of just playing music from a speaker, I put on a lo-fi mix on our TV. Like most music videos of this kind, it featured a drawn wallpaper image. In the background, there were two cute hamsters, sitting, sipping tea from their cups.
It’t’he hamsters, one of my friends said: “Oh, look! Two hamsters!” That’s when I realized: It’s not just the music. It’s the entire scene. The music, the video, the atmosphere. That’s why lo-fi works. It’s a holistic experience. Not just a song.
I’ve been watching lo-fi mixes for years. I never noticed the hamsters before. But now that I have, I can’t unsee them. That’s the thing about the background: It’s always there, even when we don’t see it. It’s only a matter of time before it reveals itself.
Don’t forget the background. Whether you’re designing an experience or trying to enjoy one, remember the hamsters in the background.

### Title: Wooden Boxes

### Content: 
Last summer, I went for a hike. At the top of the mountain, there was the obligatory hut for rest and nourishment, but also a tiny chapel. I went inside and, on the left-hand wall, there was a wooden box. Kind of like a picture frame, but deeper, and with a simple pane of glass to protect its contents.
Inside the box, there were three little figurines: a man, a woman, and a child. They were dressed in traditional clothing and stood next to a small wooden sled. There was also a tiny cross on a chain, a few coins, and a piece of paper.
The paper was folded in half, and on the outside, it said: “My name is Anna. I am 8 years old. I love my family.” On the inside, it said: “I hope my mom and dad will come back soon. I miss them so much. I am scared.”
I was so taken aback by this little piece of art, I took a picture of it. I thought about it for days. Who put it there? Why? What is the story behind it? What happened to Anna? Was she okay? I’ll never know, of course, but the box was a powerful reminder: There’s a story behind every story.
Whether you see the wooden box on the wall or not, someone’s history is always right in front of you. It might be a stranger on the bus, a friend at work, or your neighbor next door. Don’t forget to look for it.

### Title: A Circle of Teaching

### Content: 
Yesterday, I showed my fiancée a bratwurst stall that I used to go to as a child when we went shopping in a certain town. Fresh rolls, lightly charred sausages—still a classic! After the salesman handed over the goods, I looked around for ketchup and mustard. I conveniently found them beside the stall.
The’t was a small, old-fashioned stand. The kind that’s made out of wood and metal and only has a few knobs to control the temperature and flow of the sauce. I turned the ketchup knob, and nothing happened. I tried again, harder. Still nothing. I went to the mustard, and that didn’t work either. I turned both knobs a few times, but it seemed the machine was empty.
I walked back to my fiancée and said: “I don’t think it works. Let’s eat them without sauce.” “You can’t eat bratwurst without sauce!” she said. “You have to try again!” So I did. I turned the knobs some more, and then, lo and behold, a tiny drop of ketchup fell into the tray. I tried again, and this time, a small dollop of mustard came out. Success!
I was about to put the sauces on our rolls when my fiancée said: “You have to show me how it works!” I did, and then I told her: “You know, you can’t eat bratwurst without sauce.” “Yes, I do now!” she said. “Thank you for teaching me!”
That’s how life works. We learn from each other, and then we teach each other. It’s a never-ending circle, and it’s how we get to enjoy the best things in life. A bratwurst stall from our childhood, a new kind of sauce, or a new way of looking at the world. We’re all students and teachers, and we’re all here to share the best parts of our lives with one another.
Don’t forget to show someone how the sauce machine works.

### Title: How To Walk Away

### Content: 
Arcane is a critically acclaimed, animated TV series set in the League of Legends universe. Two sisters represent two warring factions of what is, essentially, the same city. Except overground, Piltover houses the rich in shiny houses and a prosperous environment, whereas underground, Zaun is marked by a lack of infrastructure—and thus a public struggling with crime and drugs.
Towards the end of season one, the sisters meet in a bar. Vi, the older one, is a bouncer in Zaun. She’s tough, rough around the edges, and always ready for a fight. Jinx, the younger one, is a brilliant scientist, but she’s also the result of a failed experiment, and now she’s on the edge of madness. Jinx is about to start a war between the two cities. Vi tries to talk her out of it.
“Look, I know I wasn’t around much growing up, but I was always watching. I saw you. You were the smartest, kindest, funniest person I ever met. I don’t know what happened to you, but I know you can walk away from this.”
Jinx is furious. She screams at her sister. “I can’t!” she yells. “I can’t walk away from this!”
Then, she turns around and starts the war.
The next time we see Jinx, she’s in a new hideout, building a giant, rocket-like weapon. As she finishes the device, she looks at herself in a mirror. She’s dressed in a new outfit. She’s wearing makeup. And she has a new hairdo.
“Look who’s walking away,” Jinx says. “Look who’s walking away.”
It’s a moment of triumph. A moment of liberation. Jinx has finally walked away from her past. From her sister. From her family. From her identity. She’s a new person now, and she’s ready to fight for what she believes in.

Walking away is hard. It’s not something you can do overnight. You can’t just wake up one day and decide to walk away from your past. It takes time. It takes effort. It takes a lot of pain.

Walking away is hard. But it’s also necessary. It’s the only way to move forward. The only way to grow. The only way to become the person you want to be.

### Title: The Phone Will Fall Again

### Content: 
Five years after my last one, I bought a new iPhone. I wasn’t overly excited. There were three reasons.
First, the new model was bigger, faster, and stronger. I mean, duh. That’s what you do with new models. But if you’ve had the last one, you also know the new one won’t be twice as good. It’ll be 10% better, 20% faster, 30% stronger — and that’s not enough to get me excited.
Second, I was already using a bigger, faster, stronger phone. My girlfriend had an iPhone 13 Pro Max, and I was using it for work. It was the exact same phone I was about to buy. I already knew what it could do, and I already knew what it couldn’t do. The latter list was longer than the former, and so I wasn’t excited.
Third, I knew the phone would fall again. I had dropped my iPhone 11 Pro many times. The screen was cracked, and the edges were dented. I was sure my new phone would suffer the same fate. It’s just a matter of time. So why get excited about something that’s about to break?
I was wrong. I was wrong about all of it. The new phone is twice as good. The screen is brighter. The speakers are louder. The battery lasts twice as long. The camera is so much better. It’s not just a new phone. It’s a new experience.
I was wrong about already knowing what it could do. The 13 Pro Max I was using had a screen protector and a case. The new phone doesn’t. It’s so much lighter. It feels like a feather in your hand. It’s a different device altogether.
I was wrong about the phone falling again. I bought a new case and a new screen protector. I’m much more careful with it. I haven’t dropped it once in the three months I’ve had it. I’m treating it with respect, and so far, it’s holding up.
The point is not that I was wrong. It’s that I was wrong about being wrong. I didn’t expect any of this. I didn’t expect to be pleasantly surprised. But I was. Life is like that. You never know what’s coming. You can’t. That’s why it’s called life. Not knowing is the whole point.
Don’t get so hung up on what you think you know that you forget there’s always something new to learn. The phone will fall again, but today, it’s still shiny and new. Enjoy the moment. You never know when it’ll be the last one.

The intro of Trigun, an anime from 1998, shows a badass guy with spiky blond hair on a distant, deserted planet, walking around in a cool red coat and slinging a massive gun. As soon as the show begins, however, all of the macho-action vibes fade away.

The monster laughs. “I’m not letting her go. I’m gonna kill her, and you’re gonna watch!” “Please,” Vash begs, “don’t do it. Let her go.” The monster laughs again, and then, he snaps the girl’s neck.

Vash is the kind of guy who never gives up. He’s the kind of guy who always tries to find a peaceful solution. He’s the kind of guy who always looks for the best in people. When my new co-worker told me she loved the Berlin nightlife, I tried to remember the last time I went to a club. It took me a solid ten minutes. I realized I had even been to one last year during a bachelor party—but before then? No clue.
There’t even remember the last time I went to a club. I don’t miss it.
I’m 33, and I guess it’s normal to grow out of certain things. But the clubbing scene? That’s something I never really grew into. I went to my first club when I was 21, and I only went because it was the only place you could legally drink in the US. I was studying abroad in Texas, and I was a student, so I didn’t have much money. The clubs were cheap, and the beer was free. The music was loud, the people were sweaty, and it was all a bit too much.
But I went, and I had fun. I met new people, and I learned how to dance. I even had a few flings. But after a while, I started to realize that I didn’t really enjoy it. I didn’t like the music, I didn’t like the crowds, and I didn’t like the fact that I had to shout to be heard.
So I stopped going. I found other ways to have fun. I went to bars, I went to concerts, and I went to parties. I even started hosting my own parties. I had a great time, and I didn’t miss the clubs at all.
Now, 12 years later, I’m a different person. I’m married, I have a job, and I have a house. I don’t go out as much as I used to, and I don’t drink as much as I used to. But I still have fun. I still go to bars, I still go to concerts, and I still go to parties. I just don’t go to clubs.
And you know what? I don’t miss it. I don’t miss the loud music, I don’t miss the sweaty crowds, and I don’t miss the shouting. I’m happy where I am, and I’m happy with who I am.
So if you’re someone who loves the clubbing scene, that’s great. Enjoy it while you can. But if you’re someone like me, who never really fit in, don’t worry. You’ll find your own way to have fun, and you’ll be just fine.
Here’s to growing up and finding your own path. Cheers!

### Title: Anchored

### Content: 
When you join the crypto industry, people will warn you: “This space is 24/7/365. Be careful. Don’t get sucked in too far, or you’ll burn out quickly.” It’s true. Thankfully, I already did all of that in 2017.
After 2018’s bear market, I didn’t want to be so obsessed with crypto again. But it’s hard to let go. I love the industry. I love the people. I love the technology. But I also love my family, my friends, and my hobbies. I want to make room for all of it.
That’s why I’m anchoring myself. I’m trying to stay in the present moment, no matter where I am. When I’m at home, I’m at home. When I’m at work, I’m at work. When I’m with my girlfriend, I’m with my girlfriend. And when I’m with my parents, I’m with my parents.
It’s hard to stay anchored. We’re always pulled in so many directions. But when you manage to do it, it feels like you’re on vacation. You can take a break from all the other places you’re supposed to be, and just enjoy the one you’re in. That’s the kind of life I want to live.
I don’t know if I’ll be able to do it forever, but I’m going to try. I want to be present for the people and things that matter to me. I want to be there for my family, my friends, and my work. And I want to enjoy the moment while it lasts.
I’m not sure if it’s the right thing to do, but it feels like the right thing to do. And that’s good enough for me.

### Title: Running for the Train

### Content: 
Most people are surprised to find out German trains aren’t particularly on time. Last year, it was only around 60% of them. Granted, most delays are only a matter of minutes, but it is usually with those minutes that the system will drive you to the brink of insanity, because many long-distance journeys include switching trains at least once.
When you’re waiting for a train that’s 7 minutes late, and you only have 10 minutes to catch the next one, you’re not going to be able to sit still. You’ll be biting your nails, checking the board every minute, and once the train finally arrives, you’ll be the first to board, hoping to get out as fast on the other end. When you finally arrive at your destination, you’ll be sweaty, exhausted, and likely behind schedule. But hey, you made it!
Of course, there’s also the alternative: You can sit down, wait, and enjoy the extra seven minutes. You can read a book, listen to a podcast, or just take a moment to breathe. You’ll still have to run for your next train, but you’ll do so from a place of calm instead of a place of frenzy. You’ll still be sweaty and exhausted, but you’ll feel a lot better about the situation.
Life is full of trains we must catch. Sometimes, we can afford to wait. Sometimes, we can’t. But we can always choose to run from a place of calm. To not let the external circumstances dictate our inner state. We can wait for the train, and when the time comes, we’ll run for it — but we’ll do it with a smile on our face.

### Title: Good People

### Content: 
Those are the ones we seek, aren’t they? But what does “good” mean? Three examples, one lesson.
Yesterday,, three examples, one lesson.
When my girlfriend and I visited a restaurant, the waiter gave us the usual spiel: “We have this, we have that, we have that, and we have this.” Then, he said: “And we also have a dish with pork belly, but it’s not on the menu, and I don’t recommend it. It’s not very good. You should get one of the other dishes.”
The waiter had no reason to say that. He could have tried to sell us the pork belly dish. He could have pretended it was a great dish. He could have stayed quiet. Instead, he told us the truth. He told us what was best for us, not what was best for him.
Good people give you the truth when it matters.
A few weeks ago, I had a problem with my tax return. I called the hotline, and a man answered. He explained the situation to me and said: “This is what happened. This is what we did. This is what you need to do.”
Then, he said: “I can see you’re not happy. I’m sorry. But this is the process. If you don’t do it, you’ll get a reminder. If you don’t do it then, you’ll get a fine. I’m sorry. I wish I could do more for you. But this is the process. I hope you have a good day.”
Good people apologize when it matters.
When I was in high school, I had a teacher who taught us about the Holocaust. He had been to Auschwitz, and he showed us pictures. He told us stories. He made us understand the magnitude of it. The scale of it. The humanity of it.
He also told us that, after the war, there was a big trial in Nuremberg, where the people who had been responsible for it were brought to justice. Then, he said: “But you know what? I don’t think any of them were really guilty. I think they were just people like you and me. They were just trying to survive. They were just trying to do their job. They were just trying to get through the day. And then, they woke up one day, and they were in hell. I don’t think any of them were really guilty. I think they were just people like you and me.”
Good people make you understand when it matters.
Good people tell you the truth, and they apologize when they can’t. Good people help you understand, and they don’t judge you for it. Good people are the ones we seek, and they’re the only ones worth seeking.
Look for good people.

### Title: Full Pockets

### Content: 
I’m about to go on my first business trip as an employee. Doing my usual “what do I have on me?” check before I leave, I realized: I now carry even more stuff in my pockets than usual. There are my phone, my keys, and my wallet. But now there’s also my work phone and my Airpods. It makes me feel a bit…bulky. So I guess some things will have to go into my backpack.
It’s interesting how, even when we’re not going anywhere, we can still carry too much. I can feel the difference between one phone and two phones. Between one set of keys and two sets of keys. I’m not sure I’ve ever felt the difference between no keys and one set of keys, but I’m sure there’s one. Maybe it’s time to let go of some of that stuff.
In any case, the next time you feel like you’re carrying the world on your shoulders, take a moment to check your pockets. You might find you can leave some of it behind.

### Title: Dosed Communication

### Content: 
After I came back from my business trip, I was exhausted. It had only been 40 hours, but with much time on the move, little sleep, and lots of information to process—all on top of actual work—I felt I had hit my cap for the week.
Thankfully, it was a short week, and so I decided to do the minimum. I showed up, did what I had to do, and then went home. No more, no less. It was a good decision. I recovered quickly and felt much better the next day.
I also took it easy on my communication. I didn’t message everyone to tell them I was back. I didn’t reach out to friends to check in. I just took care of the most urgent stuff, and that was enough. I dosed my communication, and I think that’s a good habit.
It’s easy to feel like you have to respond to every single message you receive. You don’t. You can answer one out of three, and if you’re busy, that’s perfectly fine. People will understand. They’re busy too. It’s okay to let the world spin without you for a day or two. Or three. Or even a week. The sun will still rise tomorrow, and so will you.
Don’t feel bad for dosing your communication. It’s a good thing. It’ll make your interactions more meaningful and allow you to take care of yourself.

### Title: An Answerless World

### Content: 
A recurring theme of my 30s has been realizing how clueless I am about most things. In my 20s, I seemed to have more answers. The answers, of course, came almost exclusively from other people. It was naive to latch on to them, but at least it was easy. It helped me live with conviction, if only ever for a short period of time.
What’s more, I had a lot of conviction. I was a staunch vegetarian, a dedicated runner, and a vocal supporter of my favorite artists. Now, I’m a part-time meat-eater, an on-and-off runner, and I don’t really care who’s hot and who’s not. I don’t know what the right answers are, and so I just try to live without them.
The world has always been an answerless place. It’s just that when you’re young, you don’t know it yet. You have to grow into it. The answers you receive from others are merely placeholders, but you can’t tell they’re temporary. Sooner or later, you’ll find out, and then you’ll have to make your own way.
It’s hard to live in an answerless world. It’s scary, too. But it’s also liberating. Now, you’re free to make your own rules. You can invent your own path. You can live your own life instead of someone else’s. You’ll have to keep adjusting, of course. The answers will keep changing, and so will you. But that’s the deal we’re all making when we sign up to be here, and it’s the best deal we’ll ever get.
Don’t worry about the answers. Worry about the questions. Keep asking them, and you’ll always be on the right path.

### Title: From an Eternal Point of View

### Content: 
One word which repeatedly grabbed me in Hermann Hesse’s Der Steppenwolf was “ eternity.” Hesse used it in a strange but comforting way. As if to say, “Don’t worry, there’s always eternity!” And even though eternity is not something accessible to us, every time I read about it in the book, it still felt soothing to think about it. Odd, isn’t it?
As a writer, I’m always looking for new words, and I’m not sure I’ll ever use this one, but it did get me thinking: What does it mean to look at life from an eternal point of view? Is it possible? Is it even desirable? And if so, how can we achieve it?
The most obvious consequence of eternity is that everything is temporary. The universe, the earth, and the human race will all end some day. That’s a hard pill to swallow, but it also makes life easier. If nothing is permanent, then nothing is worth getting too worked up about. Everything will pass. Even the biggest disaster, the worst tragedy, the most painful loss will eventually fade away. So will the best moments, the greatest joys, and the most exciting events.
When we see life as a series of temporary events, we can accept it more easily. We can enjoy the good times and be less afraid of the bad times. We can appreciate the present moment without worrying too much about the future or regretting the past.
Another consequence of eternity is that time is relative. A year is a long time for a human, but a short time for a tree. A century is a long time for a civilization, but a short time for the earth. A million years is a long time for the universe, but a short time for eternity.
When we see time as relative, we can be more patient. We can wait for things to happen in their own time. We can trust that everything will happen when it is meant to happen. We can also be more flexible. We can adapt to changing circumstances. We can learn from our mistakes and try again.
A third consequence of eternity is that everything is connected. Everything is part of a larger whole. Everything has a meaning and a purpose. Everything is part of a grand design.
When we see everything as connected, we can be more humble. We can recognize that we are not the center of the universe. We can respect other people, animals, plants, and things. We can also be more grateful. We can appreciate the beauty and wonder of life. We can see the good in everything and everyone.
A fourth consequence of eternity is that everything is changing. Everything is in a state of flux. Everything is transforming from one form to another.
When we see everything as changing, we can be more open-minded. We can accept new ideas and perspectives. We can learn from our experiences and grow as individuals. We can also be more creative. We can imagine new possibilities and solutions. We can invent new things and improve existing ones.
A fifth consequence of eternity is that everything is perfect. Everything is exactly as it should be. Everything is part of a divine plan.
When we see everything as perfect, we can be more peaceful. We can accept ourselves and others as they are. We can let go of our judgments and criticisms. We can also be more loving. We can treat ourselves and others with kindness and compassion. We can forgive ourselves and others for our mistakes and shortcomings.
A sixth consequence of eternity is that everything is one. Everything is part of a single consciousness. Everything is connected to a higher power.
When we see everything as one, we can be more spiritual. We can connect with our inner selves and with the universe. We can feel a sense of unity and harmony. We can also be more ethical. We can act in accordance with our values and principles. We can treat others with respect and dignity.
A seventh consequence of eternity is that everything is free. Everything is available to us. Everything is ours to use and enjoy.
When we see everything as free, we can be more generous. We can share our resources and talents with others. We can help those in need and make a positive impact on the world. We can also be more responsible. We can take care of ourselves and others. We can protect the environment and preserve the planet for future generations.
A final consequence of eternity is that everything is possible. Everything is within our reach. Everything is achievable with enough time and effort.
When we see everything as possible, we can be more optimistic. We can believe in ourselves and our abilities. We can set goals and work towards them. We can also be more persistent. We can overcome obstacles and challenges. We can learn from our failures and try again.
In conclusion, looking at life from an eternal point of view can have many benefits. It can help us be more accepting, patient, humble, grateful, open-minded, creative, peaceful, loving, spiritual, ethical, generous, responsible, optimistic, and persistent. It can also help us find meaning and purpose in life, and connect with ourselves and others.
However, looking at life from an eternal point of view is not always easy. It requires us to let go of our ego, our attachments, and our fears. It requires us to trust in the universe and have faith in ourselves. It requires us to be present in the moment and enjoy the journey.
Looking at life from an eternal point of view is not a destination, but a way of living. It is a choice that we can make every day, and that can bring us more joy, peace, and fulfillment. It is a perspective that can help us live our best lives and make a positive difference in the world.
So, what do you think? Are you ready to look at life from an eternal point of view?

### Title: It’s Still Chocolate

### Content: 
A few days ago, I miraculously got my hands on some original Dubai chocolate. A friend happens to live there, and his girlfriend kindly brought me a bar while she was in town. “Tell me what you think,” he texted me, “but I believe you and I will agree.”
Based’t know, but my friend is a hardcore dark chocolate fan. 70% cocoa and above. He can’t stand anything else. “It’s just too sweet,” he says. And yet, he brought me milk chocolate.
“Maybe it’s not that sweet?” I wondered. As it turns out, it’s not. I think it’s the best milk chocolate I’ve ever had. Not too sweet, not too bitter. A perfect balance of flavors. It’s also not cheap. At 12 euros for 100 grams, it’s more expensive than even the most expensive Lindt chocolate.
As I was chewing on a piece, however, I realized: “It’s still chocolate. It’s still the same product. Just a different version of it.” And while I can see why someone might pay 12 euros for a bar of chocolate, I can also see why someone might pay 50 cents. It’s still chocolate. And it’s the same product.
The lesson here is twofold: First, you can’t put a price on taste. If you love something, you’ll gladly pay more for a better version of it. Second, if you’re selling a commodity, it’s hard to charge a premium for it. It’s still chocolate. It’s still coffee. It’s still a T-shirt.
There’s a saying that “you can’t polish a turd.” It’s true. But you can also only put so much glitter on gold. Be careful what you sell, and be careful what you buy.

### Title: Reaching the Top 4

### Content: 
In the original and most subsequent Pokémon games, the endgame is to defeat your childhood rival—but not before you’ve made it past the Elite Four, or “Top Four” in German. They were the toughest Pokémon trainers in the game, and you better came prepared. In fact, you had to pass a whole set of separate trials along Victory Road just to get there.
Whenever I think of “the top,” the people I aspire to be like in one way or another, I think of them as the Elite Four. The people I want to be like in business, the people I want to be like in writing, the people I want to be like in relationships, they’re all the Elite Four. I’m not sure there are always four of them, but I’m sure there’s always more than one. A single role model is easy to copy, but what if they’re wrong? What if they’re a bad example? It’s good to have multiple points of reference to compare and contrast.
The point of the Elite Four, however, was not to defeat them. It was to become one of them. Once you’ve beaten the game, you can do it again and again and again. That’s the real fun. The real challenge. To be the best of the best, you must keep playing. You must keep trying. You must keep training. If you’re not up for it, you’ll be replaced. The Elite Four is not a static group of people. It’s a rotating club of those who are at the top of their game at any given time. If you want to stay there, you must keep playing. Keep trying. Keep training.
The next time you think about who you want to be like, think about the Elite Four. Who are your role models? Who do you want to be like? Who are the people you aspire to be like in one way or another? Then, remember: The point is not to defeat them. The point is to become one of them.
